The transformation is **C=O ⟶ CH₂**: the ketone of the acetyl group is reduced all the way to
a methylene, while the **hydroxyl on the ring survives untouched**.
Two named reactions do this conversion, and the choice between them is decided by what else
is in the molecule:
**Clemmensen reduction** — Zn-Hg with **concentrated HCl**, strongly **acidic**
**Wolff–Kishner reduction** — hydrazine then KOH in ethylene glycol at ~180 °C, strongly
**basic**
Here the substrate carries a **secondary alcohol** on the ring. Under Clemmensen's hot
concentrated acid that alcohol would be protonated and **dehydrated** to an alkene, so the
acidic route is unsuitable. The **basic** Wolff–Kishner conditions leave the hydroxyl alone ✓
— option (b).
The mechanism: the ketone condenses with hydrazine to the hydrazone, and the strong base then
removes a proton and expels **N₂**, leaving the carbanion which picks up a proton to give the
CH₂.
Why not the others:
**(c) Ni/H₂** reduces C=C readily but needs forcing conditions for a ketone, and would give
the **alcohol**, not CH₂.
**(d) NaBH₄** reduces the ketone only as far as the **secondary alcohol**.
The rule in a line: **acid-sensitive substrate ⟶ Wolff–Kishner; base-sensitive substrate ⟶
Clemmensen.**
∴ H₂N–NH₂, KOH/ethylene glycol.

Look at which molecule can supply the enolate.
**Benzaldehyde**, C₆H₅CHO — the carbonyl is attached to the ring and a hydrogen, so there is
**no α-hydrogen**. It cannot form an enolate; it can only act as the **electrophile**.
**Acetophenone**, C₆H₅COCH₃ — the methyl group provides **α-hydrogens**, so dilute NaOH can
remove one and generate the **enolate**, the **nucleophile**.
So one partner supplies the nucleophile and the other the electrophile, and the reaction is
an **aldol condensation between two different carbonyl compounds** — a **cross (mixed) aldol
condensation** ✓ — option (c).
The product, after the aldol addition and loss of water, is the α,β-unsaturated ketone
C₆H₅CH=CH–CO–C₆H₅, **benzalacetophenone (chalcone)**.
Why the others are wrong:
**(d) Aldol condensation** (plain) describes **one** carbonyl compound reacting with itself;
here there are two different ones, so the reaction is specifically a *cross* aldol.
**(a) and (b) Cannizzaro** requires aldehydes with **no** α-hydrogen **and** concentrated
alkali. Acetophenone has α-hydrogens, and the alkali here is dilute.
The reason this particular cross aldol gives a single clean product is that only one of the
two partners can enolise — which is the condition that makes a mixed aldol useful.
∴ cross aldol condensation.

In a cross aldol, the **nucleophile** supplies the enolate and the **electrophile** supplies
the carbonyl that is attacked. The question fixes both roles.
**Nucleophile — butanal**, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO. Base removes an α-hydrogen from **C-2**, the CH₂
next to the CHO, giving a carbanion there. That carbon carries an **ethyl** group.
**Electrophile — propanal**, CH₃CH₂CHO. Its carbonyl carbon is attacked.
**The bond formed** joins butanal's C-2 to propanal's carbonyl carbon, and the carbonyl oxygen
becomes an –OH:
CH₃CH₂–**CH(OH)**–**CH(C₂H₅)**–CHO
**Now name it.** Number from the aldehyde:
C1 = **CHO**
C2 = CH bearing the **ethyl** group
C3 = CH bearing the **OH**
C4 = CH₂
C5 = CH₃

**2-ethyl-3-hydroxypentanal** ✓

**methyl** rather than an ethyl, and the product would be 3-hydroxy-2-methylhexanal —
option (b). Reading which compound is named the nucleophile is the whole question.
∴ 2-ethyl-3-hydroxypentanal.

The benzoin condensation is the dimerisation of two benzaldehyde molecules, catalysed
specifically by **cyanide ion** — and the mechanism explains why no other catalyst will do.
**Step 1 — cyanide adds** to the carbonyl carbon, giving the cyanohydrin alkoxide, which
picks up a proton:
Ph–CHO + CN⁻ ⟶ Ph–CH(O⁻)–CN ⟶ Ph–CH(OH)–CN
**Step 2 — the key step.** The hydrogen on that carbon is now **acidic**, because the carbanion
left behind is stabilised by the adjacent **–CN** group, which withdraws electrons and
delocalises the charge onto its nitrogen. Removing it gives
**Ph–C⁻(OH)–CN** ✓ — option (c), the intermediate the question asks for
**Step 3** — that carbanion attacks a second molecule of benzaldehyde, and loss of CN⁻
finally gives benzoin, PhCH(OH)COPh.
This is the whole point of using cyanide: it is a good nucleophile, it makes the adjacent C–H
acidic, and it is a good **leaving group** at the end, so it is regenerated as a catalyst. No
other simple anion does all three.
The distractors are the wrong charge or the wrong species: (b) is the same structure as a
**cation**, which no base could produce; (a) and (d) are acylium and acyl anion fragments
that play no part here.
∴ Ph–C⁻(OH)CN.

The Cannizzaro reaction is the **disproportionation** of an aldehyde with no α-hydrogen in
concentrated alkali: one molecule is reduced to the alcohol, another oxidised to the
carboxylate.
The mechanism runs in three steps:
**Step 1** — hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide
PhCH(O⁻)OH. **Fast**, as nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl usually is.
**Step 2** — that intermediate transfers a **hydride ion (H⁻)** from its carbon to the
carbonyl carbon of a **second** benzaldehyde molecule. **Slow** ✓ — this is the
**rate-determining** step.
**Step 3** — proton exchange between the alkoxide formed and the acid gives the final
alcohol and carboxylate. **Fast**, as proton transfers between oxygens always are.
Why step 2 is slow: a **hydride ion is a very poor leaving group**, carrying a full negative
charge on a bare hydrogen, and it has to move between two carbon atoms with no help from a
solvent. Everything else in the mechanism is either an addition to a carbonyl or a proton
hop, both of which are fast.
The experimental evidence is that the reaction is **second order in aldehyde** and first
order in hydroxide — consistent with two aldehyde molecules being involved by the slow step,
which is exactly the hydride transfer.
∴ the transfer of hydride ion to the carbonyl group.

The Cannizzaro reaction requires an aldehyde with **no α-hydrogen** — otherwise concentrated
alkali generates an enolate and the molecule undergoes **aldol** condensation instead. A
**cross** Cannizzaro needs **both** partners to lack α-hydrogens.
Check each aldehyde:
**HCHO** — the carbonyl carbon bears two hydrogens and there is no α-carbon at all. **No
α-H** ✓
**C₆H₅CHO** — the carbonyl is attached to the ring; there is no α-carbon bearing hydrogen.
**No α-H** ✓
**CH₃CHO** — the methyl group is the α-carbon and it carries **three α-hydrogens** ✗
So the only pair in which **neither** has an α-hydrogen is
**(c) C₆H₅CHO and HCHO** ✓
Options (a) and (b) both include acetaldehyde, which would simply undergo aldol condensation
in the alkali, so (d) 'all of these' fails too.
There is a further point that makes this pair the standard one. In a cross Cannizzaro the
**better hydride donor is oxidised**, and **formaldehyde is the best hydride donor of all** —
so it is reliably oxidised to formate while benzaldehyde is reduced to benzyl alcohol:
C₆H₅CHO + HCHO + NaOH ⟶ C₆H₅CH₂OH + HCOONa
That predictability is why formaldehyde is chosen as the partner whenever a cross Cannizzaro
is wanted preparatively.
∴ C₆H₅CHO, HCHO.

The product RCH₂CH₂COOH has **one more carbon** than the starting alcohol RCH₂CH₂OH, so the
route must **add a carbon**, and the nitrile route is the standard way to do it.
**Step 1 — PBr₃.** Converts the alcohol to the alkyl bromide, a good substrate for
substitution:
RCH₂CH₂OH ⟶ **RCH₂CH₂Br**
**Step 2 — KCN.** Cyanide displaces bromide by SN2, and the **–CN brings the extra carbon**:
RCH₂CH₂Br + KCN ⟶ **RCH₂CH₂CN** + KBr
**Step 3 — H⁺ (aqueous acid, with heat).** The nitrile is hydrolysed, through the amide, to
the carboxylic acid:
RCH₂CH₂CN + 2H₂O + H⁺ ⟶ **RCH₂CH₂COOH** + NH₄⁺
So the sequence is **PBr₃, KCN, H⁺** ✓ — option (a).
Why the others fail:
**(b) PBr₃, KCN, H₂** — hydrogen **reduces** the nitrile to a primary **amine**,
RCH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂, not the acid.
**(c) KCN, H⁺** — cyanide cannot displace **–OH** directly; hydroxide is a poor leaving group,
which is exactly why step 1 is needed.
**(d) HCN, PBr₃, H⁺** — HCN adds to carbonyl compounds, not to alcohols, and the order is
wrong in any case.
The general principle: to **lengthen** a carbon chain by one, go alcohol ⟶ halide ⟶ nitrile
⟶ acid.
∴ PBr₃, KCN, H⁺.

LiAlH₄ attacks the carbonyl carbon, so the reactivity order is the **general order of
reactivity of acid derivatives**, set by two things: how strongly the attached group donates
electrons into the carbonyl (which deactivates it) and how good a **leaving group** it is.
Take them in turn:
**(A) Amide, C₂H₅CONH₂** — nitrogen is the **best** electron donor by resonance, so the
carbonyl is the least electrophilic; and NH₂⁻ is a terrible leaving group. **Least reactive**
**(B) Ester, C₂H₅COOCH₃** — oxygen donates less effectively than nitrogen, and OR⁻ is a
better leaving group than NH₂⁻. More reactive than the amide
**(D) Anhydride, (C₂H₅CO)₂O** — the single oxygen must share its lone pair between **two**
carbonyls, so each gets less stabilisation; and the carboxylate released is a good leaving
group
**(C) Acid chloride, C₂H₅COCl** — chlorine is a poor π-donor (its 3p orbital overlaps the
carbon 2p badly) and Cl⁻ is an excellent leaving group. **Most reactive**
So in **increasing** reactivity:
**(A) < (B) < (D) < (C)** ✓
The order amide < ester < anhydride < acid chloride is worth memorising outright; it governs
not only reduction but hydrolysis, aminolysis and every other nucleophilic acyl substitution,
and it is why an acid chloride can be used to make any of the others but not the reverse.
∴ (A) < (B) < (D) < (C).

Decarboxylation is easy only when the molecule can pass through a **six-membered cyclic
transition state**, and that requires a **carbonyl group β to the carboxyl** — in other words,
a **β-keto acid**.
In such a compound the carboxyl O–H hydrogen reaches across to the ketone oxygen, CO₂ departs,
and an enol is left which tautomerises to the ketone. The whole thing happens on gentle
warming.
Examine the four:
**(b)** ✓ a **ring carboxylic acid with the ketone on the adjacent carbon** — the C=O is
exactly **β** to the COOH, so the six-membered transition state can form. **Decarboxylates
most readily** ✓
**(d)** has a ketone too, but the acid is **–CH₂COOH**, one carbon further out, so the
carbonyl is **γ** to the carboxyl. The cyclic transition state would have to be seven-membered
and the reaction is far harder.
**(a)** and **(c)** are **dicarboxylic** acids with no ketone at all. A plain carboxylic acid
needs soda-lime and 630 K to decarboxylate.
The β-keto acid effect is the basis of several standard reactions — the **acetoacetic ester
synthesis** ends with exactly this decarboxylation, and so does the malonic ester synthesis
(where a second carboxyl plays the role of the ketone).
It is also why β-keto acids are rarely isolated: many lose CO₂ at room temperature.
∴ option (b).
